cards.headline: Russian ballistic missile strike in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, kills 2 and wounds 60

pages.text: A Russian strike on the center of Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in central Ukraine, killed a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, according to local officials. Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, reported on Telegram that the attack began with two ballistic missiles. As emergency and rescue operations commenced, three additional rockets hit doctors, rescuers, and utility workers, Vilkul said. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, stated that 60 people were wounded, including six children.

cards.headline: Around 700,000 people displaced by conflict in southern Ethiopia

pages.text: Around 700,000 people have been displaced from their homes due to fighting in southern Ethiopia, according to the British NGO Islamic Relief. The organization reported on November 19, 2026, that clashes between members of the Oromo and Ethiopian Somali communities began in late October. The violence was reportedly sparked by a dispute over control of the southern town of Moyale, located on the border between Ethiopia and Kenya. Kedir Musema Hameza, the head of Islamic Relief's Ethiopia programme, described the situation as a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in Ethiopia's border regions. Fighting involving heavy weaponry has reportedly spread up to 300 kilometres from Moyale along the border shared by Kenya, Somalia, and Ethiopia.

Islamic Relief reported widespread destruction of businesses, petrol stations, and homes, alongside the disruption of water, sanitation, and health services. The NGO warned of a deepening humanitarian crisis and noted that accessing affected locations has been challenging. Approximately 50,000 people have fled into Kenya, which the organization says is placing additional pressure on host communities and local services. The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has not commented on the violence. This conflict occurs as Ethiopia faces multiple internal struggles, including recent fighting between government forces and rebels in Tigray, hundreds of kilometres to the north, and long-running insurgencies in the Amhara and Oromia regions that have displaced hundreds of thousands of people. Regional borders in Ethiopia, which were established by the 1995 constitution, have frequently been a source of conflict.

cards.headline: US-French man convicted of arson for deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles

pages.text: A US District Court jury in Los Angeles has convicted a 30-year-old US-French man of federal arson charges related to the 2025 Palisades fire. The fire killed 12 people and devastated the Pacific Palisades seaside enclave, destroying approximately 6,800 homes and other structures. Property losses are estimated at $150 billion (€136.7 billion). The man, a former Uber driver, is scheduled to be sentenced on March 17 and faces up to 40 years in prison, according to First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli. This verdict follows a retrial after a judge declared a mistrial in June following a previous trial that ended with a hung jury.

The jury found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025, in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. Prosecutors stated that security camera footage and cellphone location data indicated he was the only person nearby when the blaze began. While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later during fierce winds, becoming the highly destructive Palisades Fire. During both trials, prosecutors characterized the man as a loner who held a deep resentment against society and particularly the wealthy. The man was arrested in October 2025.

cards.headline: Tankers struck by projectiles in Strait of Hormuz near Oman

pages.text: The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz. One tanker was hit at its rear approximately 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on the northern coast of Oman. A second tanker was struck in its engine room approximately 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab. While no casualties were reported, it remains unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels. These developments occur as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the waterway, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the current conflict began. The conflict, involving Tehran, Washington, and Tel Aviv, started when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

Iran’s navy provided a different account, stating that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait. In a statement broadcast by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of traveling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off and ignoring warnings. This account could not be independently verified, and it is unclear if the burning tanker mentioned by the Iranian navy was involved in either of the two incidents reported by the UKMTO. Al Jazeera correspondent Resul Serdar reported in Tehran that incidents involving tankers have increased sharply over the past week. Citing statements from Iran’s armed forces, Serdar noted that about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous week, averaging roughly three a day.

cards.headline: Israeli strike kills three Palestinians in Gaza City vehicle carrying food aid

pages.text: An Israeli strike killed three Palestinians in a vehicle transporting food and supplies in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of Gaza City, according to Gaza’s civil defence and eyewitnesses. A Reuters witness reported that the vehicle appeared to be carrying packaged foodstuffs and papers featuring the logo of World Central Kitchen, an aid organization that distributes food in Gaza. Eyewitness Abu Zein Al-Daya said the vehicle was about to stop to distribute food and drink to children when it was hit by a missile. Following the strike, meals of cooked rice were scattered around the partially bloodied vehicle, according to reports from the scene.

The Israeli military stated it targeted three terrorists from the military wing of Islamic Jihad who were traveling in a van carrying food and supplies for the militant group. An Israeli military official said that, according to initial information, one of the targeted individuals had previously worked for an international aid organization but had been fired after the military provided that organization with information identifying him as a terrorist. The official stated the other two individuals were not known to have worked for international organizations and claimed the vehicle hit bore no visible markings indicating it belonged to a humanitarian aid organization. The Israeli military noted that Gazan sources identified the targets as aid workers employed by an international organization.

The strike occurred during a period following an October 2025 US-backed ceasefire that halted major fighting in the territory but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas' disarmament. Since that ceasefire, an AFP tally based on Gaza health ministry data—which the United Nations considers reliable—reports more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed. During the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers and one civilian contractor have been killed. This incident follows a 2024 strike that killed seven World Central Kitchen workers, including citizens of Australia, Britain, and Poland; the Israeli military previously cited serious errors and breaches of procedure in that instance but stated in 2026 it found no basis to open criminal investigations.

cards.headline: Tatyana Kim steps down as CEO of Russia’s Wildberries following EU sanctions

pages.text: Tatyana Kim, the head of Russia’s largest online retailer Wildberries, has stepped down, according to reports from Russian media. The TASS and RIA news agencies cited a corporate filings register stating that the company has appointed Alexei Kulikov as its new CEO. This leadership change follows the European Union's decision on November 16 to add Kim to its Russia sanctions list. Wildberries did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the transition.

The EU sanctions against Kim include an asset freeze, as well as travel and transaction bans. Brussels stated that Kim was targeted because Wildberries is one of the largest taxpayers in Russia and operates as a supply network for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and dual-use goods. Both the Kremlin and Wildberries have denied that the company supplies the Russian army.

Wildberries stated that the EU sanctions on Kim would not affect its operations, noting that the company has no assets in the EU and does not conduct business there. The company said that Wildberries and other group companies would continue to operate as usual.

cards.headline: ANC seeks power-sharing deals in South African cities following election setback

pages.text: The African National Congress (ANC) is attempting to secure power-sharing deals to maintain control of most of South Africa's cities after a significant decline in support during local elections. Although the ANC received the most votes overall at 31%, down from 46% in the previous local election, the party lost control of more than half of the councils it held in 2021. Political parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

The ANC's performance represents its worst result since the party came to power in 1994, when South Africa transitioned from apartheid to democracy. The party won a majority in only one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, which is a decrease from the six provinces it held in the last elections. In terms of major urban centers, the ANC won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared to six in 2021.

In Gauteng, South Africa's economic powerhouse, the pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) won the most votes in Johannesburg, Pretoria, and the Ekurhuleni region. Nationally, the DA received 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago. The DA also retained its majority in Cape Town and won the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, the location of Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth). The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, placed third with 10% of the vote.

cards.headline: Russian cargo ship struck by drones in Gulf of Finland

pages.text: A Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, was struck by two drones in the Gulf of Finland, according to reports from Russian and Finnish authorities. The ship, which is bound for Kaliningrad, was reportedly attacked three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, according to Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of Russia’s Leningrad region. The Finnish Defence Forces stated by afternoon that the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. The Sparta II is a roll-on-roll-off ship built in 2000 that sails under a Russian flag. Finnish authorities say the vessel has links to Russia’s armed forces and has drifted into territorial waters off the southern coast of Finland. The attack occurred west of Gogland Island, off the coast of the Finnish town of Loviisa. While there is no confirmed information regarding the ship's cargo, Iljin stated that it cannot be ruled out that military materiel is on board.

cards.headline: Three Chittagong Education Board employees arrested for allegedly forging SSC exam results

pages.text: The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of police arrested three employees of the Chittagong Education Board in Bangladesh for their alleged involvement in forging Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examination results. A team from the CID's Dhaka Metro Heinous Crime unit arrested the individuals on the night of November 18, 2026, and handed them over to the Panchlaish Police Station, according to reports from UNB cited by The Financial Express. The arrestees include computer division programmer Md. Abdul Malek and scanning division staff Farhadul Islam and Shahidul Alam Jisan. Some of the accused had held their positions for 13 years.

A case filed by the Board Secretary alleges the accused altered marks to pass a student who had originally failed in 10 subjects during the 2026 SSC exams. The forgery involved drastically inflating scores across multiple subjects, such as raising a Mathematics score from 9 to 66, a Higher Mathematics score from 0 to 46, and a Chemistry score from 1 to 46. Inspector Russell stated that a probe is underway to determine if other individuals were involved, noting that questions remain regarding an earlier, unaccepted HSC forgery charge sheet.

cards.headline: Haitian police and El Salvador troops reconquer Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince

pages.text: Haitian police and troops from El Salvador have reconquered the Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince, a facility that had fallen under the control of heavily armed gangs in 2024. The stadium, named after an athlete who won a silver medal at the 1928 Olympics, had been used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss known as Izo. The loss of the stadium contributed to the displacement of Haiti's national football team, the Grenadiers, who were forced to play World Cup qualifying games abroad because they no longer had a home pitch.

Nayib Bukele, the authoritarian president of El Salvador, has sent more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti since mid-October. Bukele claimed that forces now have the upper hand on the ground, describing the military movement as a step toward ending a criminal insurrection that has killed thousands of people and displaced more than 1.5 million people. While some citizens have expressed hope, others fear the ongoing offensive could exacerbate the country's volatile situation.

In Port-au-Prince, some residents celebrated the arrival of the foreign troops. Bòs Baton, a 55-year-old decorator, expressed hope for the country's future outside the stadium. Baton recalled being driven from the Poste-Marchand area after criminals set his home on fire during an armed uprising that began in February 2024.

cards.headline: Illegal mining pollution keeps Kyebi water treatment plant shut for more than a year

pages.text: The Ghana Water Limited (GWL) Kyebi Water Treatment Plant in the Abuakwa South Municipality of the Eastern Region has remained shut for more than a year due to severe pollution of the Birim River caused by illegal mining, known as galamsey. This shutdown has deprived residents of Kyebi and surrounding communities of treated water, forcing many to rely on alternative sources such as wells and boreholes for their daily needs. The Birim River serves as the main source of raw water for the facility. Dr Shafic Suleman, Executive Secretary of the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC), stated during a media briefing in Koforidua that the pollution has overwhelmed the plant. He noted that the facility's main intake source, a mountain spring located approximately seven kilometres from active illegal mining sites, has also been heavily polluted, resulting in high turbidity and iron levels.

The pollution from illegal mining has significantly increased the turbidity of the river, making water treatment extremely difficult and expensive. Turbidity refers to the cloudiness or haziness of a fluid caused by large numbers of individual particles. At the raw water intake point, turbidity levels have reached more than 63 million Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), which far exceeds the plant's original design capacity of 200 NTU. GWL had previously warned that these high turbidity levels made treatment costly and created a risk of damaging equipment if pumping operations continued. Dr Suleman reported that because the plant is shut, residents are using boreholes and wells, some of which contain high levels of iron. He called on the residents and chiefs of Kyebi to help stop illegal mining in the area to protect the Birim River and other water bodies from further pollution.

Regarding service performance in the region over the past year, Dr Suleman said the PURC received 1,330 complaints from consumers of the Ghana Water Limited and the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG). Of those, 1,306 complaints, or 98.2 per cent, had been resolved. The complaints primarily involved billing discrepancies, metering problems, low voltage, erratic power supply, and service delivery challenges. Dr Suleman also noted that power fluctuations occurring between 7 p.m. and 8 p.m. have disrupted water treatment and distribution in both Kyebi and Koforidua.

cards.headline: New fossil civet species named after Abu Dhabi discovered in UAE

pages.text: Palaeontologists have discovered a new species of carnivore that lived approximately seven million years ago at a fossil site in the Al Dhafra region of Abu Dhabi. The creature, a type of civet, has been named *Promegaviverra abudhabiensis* after the emirate. This discovery represents the first viverrid—a family of carnivores that includes civets and genets—found on the Arabian Peninsula. Scientists believe the animal, which may have weighed at least 20kg, provides evidence that giant civets migrated through ancient Arabia from Asia to Africa.

The fossil was identified from a right hemimandible, or lower jaw, composed of four fragments found on Shuweihat Island, located about 265km west of Abu Dhabi city. Hanneke Jacobs, a collections management senior specialist at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, discovered the first fragment of the jawbone at the Shuweihat 2 fossil site in late February. Following an intensive search, a team including Dr. Mark Beech, the museum’s head of geoscience, and Dr. Luca Bellucci, the museum’s palaeontology curator, found three additional fragments within approximately one metre of the original find. The four pieces were then fitted together to form the jawbone. While researchers initially suspected the specimen might belong to a wolverine, they determined the teeth were different from those of a wolverine.

cards.headline: University of Ghana student representatives reject 15% hostel fee increase

pages.text: The University of Ghana Students’ Representative Council (UGSRC) has rejected a 15 per cent increase in hostel fees, arguing the hike does not reflect the financial difficulties of students and their parents. The UGSRC is calling on university management and University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL) to review the proposed increment downwards to maintain affordability. This adjustment would increase the annual accommodation fee for students in the four Diaspora halls from GH¢7,000 to GH¢8,050. The 15 per cent figure follows a reduction from an initial 26 per cent increase proposed by UGEL, which was announced after a meeting involving the UGSRC, the Junior Common Room (JCR) executives, and the Graduate Students’ Association of Ghana (GRASAG). On November 20, 2026, UGSRC President Abraham Kofi Amudzegbe cautioned private hostel operators against prioritizing business profits over student welfare, stating that unaffordable accommodation could negatively impact academic work and mental health.

In addition to opposing the fee hike, the UGSRC is demanding stronger regulation of private hostel charges around the Legon campus. The council wants the university to establish a framework that includes an approved threshold for rent increases, a defined academic-year calendar for adjustments, and an enforceable Rent Control mechanism to prevent arbitrary increases by private operators. The UGSRC has also petitioned the Rent Control Department for intervention. Rent Control Commissioner Frederick Opoku has stepped in after inspecting hostel facilities and being confronted by some hostel managers. Mr. Opoku has petitioned the Attorney General to grant him prosecutorial powers to address recalcitrant landlords.

cards.headline: Hybrid crabs outnumber snow crabs in Bering Sea surveys

pages.text: Commercially sized hybrid adult male crabs now outnumber snow crabs in parts of the Bering Sea, according to a 2026 survey. These hybrids are a cross between snow crabs—a species of spider crab that can grow up to a metre wide—and their larger relatives, the tanner crabs. The emergence of these hybrids follows an extreme heatwave in 2018 and 2019 that left the Bering Sea nearly ice-free by early spring and killed 10bn snow crabs. While researchers previously found hybrids in areas where the ranges of the two species overlap, they were considered a rarity until recently. In 2025, researchers recorded more than 13 times more hybrids than the historical average, and the 2026 survey indicates this increase is continuing.

The hybrid crabs possess physical characteristics from both parent species. They feature a squashed M-shape in the mouth, which is a combination of the flat mouth of snow crabs and the distinctive M-shape of tanner crabs, as well as a mix of red and green eyes. Erin Fedewa, a biologist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Alaska Fisheries Science Center, noted that the hybrids were immediately apparent during sampling. While it often takes several years of survey data to understand such biological shifts, Fedewa stated that seeing large male hybrids at the first sampling station served as an affirmation of the trend.

cards.headline: Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says

pages.text: The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) stated that Israeli authorities have not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers or ensure they can safely reach their groves. Citing the Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory—a group comprising UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs—Ocha reported that in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, most of which were olives.

The Humanitarian Country Team also reported that more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in property damage or casualties, including damage to more than 4,000 trees and saplings. The team noted that this number of attacks exceeds any previously recorded olive harvest season. While the team stated the harvesting window is closing, they noted there is still time to act. Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies have urged Israeli authorities to end attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, ensure farmers have free, safe, sufficient, and reliable access to their land, and hold perpetrators accountable as required by international law.

cards.headline: Infant death in Palakkad, Kerala, highlights medical and financial struggles in tribal settlements

pages.text: Dakshina, an infant from the Vechapathi hamlet in the Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district, died on April 13, 2026, following medical complications. Her death is part of a series of 10 reported infant deaths in Attappadi, a predominantly tribal settlement in Kerala, India. Dakshina was born on June 13, 2025, and doctors detected a hole in her heart when she was five months old.

After being taken to several hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, surgery was ruled out for Dakshina. She was referred to a cooperative hospital in Perinthalmanna, Malappuram district, which is approximately a two-and-a-half-hour drive from her home. Dakshina's parents, Minnal Rani and Chandra Sekhar, stated that the hospital refused to release their daughter's body until a bill of ₹10,000 was paid. They were able to raise the funds with assistance from a ward councillor.

Minnal Rani has kept a logbook of Dakshina's treatment containing ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes that she had saved for her daughter's medical expenses. Rani stated that the money will remain untouched. Dakshina was buried near a coconut tree at the family's house in Vechapathi hamlet.

cards.headline: Researchers develop method to control infrared light wavelength and polarization using twisted semiconductor layers

pages.text: A research team led by Professor Jeongyong Kim of the Department of Energy Science has developed a technology to achieve full control over the wavelength and polarization of infrared light by stacking and twisting two atomically thin semiconductor layers. The findings were published in ACS Nano. This development utilizes interlayer excitons—bound states formed when light shines on a semiconductor, causing negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes to pair up—to potentially advance ultra-low-power optoelectronic devices and quantum computing technologies. Unlike ordinary excitons, interlayer excitons (IEs) occur when electrons and holes reside in different layers of stacked semiconductors, resulting in lifetimes that are tens of times longer and easier control via external voltage.

The team addressed limitations found in conventional 2D semiconductors, which possess isotropic structural characteristics that restrict IEs to emitting light only at specific angles, such as 0° and 60°, without polarization. To overcome this, the researchers used anisotropic semiconductor materials, specifically rhenium disulfide (ReS₂) and rhenium diselenide (ReSe₂), which have optical properties that vary based on crystal orientation. By stacking two of these layers and precisely twisting them at angles ranging from 1° to 88°, the team created a moiré pattern—a wavelike pattern formed between the atomic lattices similar to the effect seen when two mesh screens overlap. This moiré structure allowed the researchers to successfully generate stable IE emission in the infrared region at virtually any twist angle.

cards.headline: Bonded labourers in India await rescue certificates and financial aid despite Supreme Court order

pages.text: Bonded labourers in India continue to struggle for rehabilitation funds and official rescue certificates despite a Supreme Court order mandating specific timelines for assistance. At a conference held at the Press Club on November 19, 2026, several survivors recounted being lured and forced to work without pay for months. These individuals originated from Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Maharashtra. Many survivors are seeking funds through the Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers, but have faced difficulties obtaining the necessary documentation to access them.

A release certificate, issued by district administrations, is an official document that formally recognizes the release of a rescued bonded labourer. This certificate makes individuals eligible for financial assistance, rehabilitation, and protection from future exploitation. Under a recent Supreme Court order, the Union government, State governments, and Union Territories are directed to ensure that bonded labourers receive financial assistance within seven days of their release certificates being issued. Additionally, rehabilitation measures must begin within 90 days of a person's rescue.

One case highlighted at the conference involved Deepika (name changed), a 17-year-old from Jharkhand. She traveled to Delhi seeking livelihood support for her farmer parents but was allegedly confined to private residences in Dwarka and Rohini, where she was deprived of her phone and cut off from her family. Her lawyer, Vinod, stated that she was rescued on October 27 from a private residence in Rohini and placed under the care of a Child Welfare Committee (CWC). Despite her rescue weeks ago, no First Information Report (FIR) has been registered against her traffickers or employers. The Deputy Commissioner of Police, Dwarka, stated that an FIR will be registered once the CWC receives her testimony regarding trafficking and possible sexual abuse.

cards.headline: U.S. government auctions 31.5 million acres of American Samoan seabed for mineral exploration

pages.text: The U.S. government has auctioned 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of the American Samoan seabed, an action that follows a federal court ruling finding the sale to be illegal and despite public opposition. The auction, which took place on Nov. 19 in Thousand Oaks, California, marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals. Wetstone U.S. Ventures secured both leases at a starting price of $3 million each, which is approximately 19 U.S. cents per acre. The auction lasted approximately 20 minutes and was publicly livestreamed. While two bidders, Wetstone U.S. Ventures and the Norwegian company Adepth, were present, only Wetstone participated in the bidding process. The two lots offered covered approximately 15 million acres and 16 million acres respectively.

The auction involves areas within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), which extends 200 nautical miles from the shore. While American Samoa, a U.S. territory, imposed a moratorium in 2024 on deep-sea mining in waters extending up to 3 nautical miles from its coastline, the U.S. government maintains jurisdiction over the remainder of the EEZ. This jurisdiction allows the U.S. to pursue seabed mineral activities in those areas without approval from the American Samoan government. Regarding the sale, American Samoa Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula released a statement on Nov. 16 calling the lease sale an “historic moment” for his nation.

cards.headline: Roman cup and 413 artifacts unearthed in 2,000-year-old Mongolian tomb

pages.text: Archaeologists have completed a four-year excavation of Tomb 160, a 2,000-year-old burial site in Duurlig Nars, Mongolia, that contained 413 artifacts. The discovery of items such as a glass cup believed to be of Roman origin suggests the nomadic Xiongnu Empire was part of a vast exchange network connecting distant powers, including the Roman Empire and the Lelang Commandery—an administrative division of China’s Han dynasty located in what is now Korea. The National Museum of Korea, the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, and the National Museum of Mongolia conducted the excavation of the site, which is part of a burial ground containing approximately 300 graves. The tomb itself measures nearly 240 feet in length, making it the largest of its kind discovered in Mongolia to date, though its interior is described as small and shallow.
